answer.label: Not George Carlin — an anonymous Vietnam-era protest slogan
answer.authorDates: In print since 19 May 1968 · Vietnam-era antiwar saying
answer.sourceLine: The line is a communal protest slogan, not a comedian’s joke: it has been in print since 19 May 1968, when Omaha’s Sunday World-Herald reported students picketing Armed Forces Day with a sign reading “Fighting for peace is like raping for love.” It appears on none of George Carlin’s albums, HBO specials or books, and the credit to him seems to have taken hold only after his death in 2008.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the wording is documented, the attribution is not.

source.excerpt: “Listen,” a corporal said to me, “we’ve got a saying here: Fighting for peace is like screwing for virginity.”
trail: 19 May 1968 — Omaha’s Sunday World-Herald reports University of Northern Iowa students picketing an Armed Forces Day observance with signs including “Fighting for peace is like raping for love” — the earliest citation in Barry Popik’s chronology ↗.

1969–1970 — the saying spreads anonymously through campus graffiti, a Chu Lai latrine wall and letters to the editor; Liberation attributes it to “an underground pundit,” and twice in this period no author is named at all (Popik ↗).
1971–1978 — it reaches print books (Eliot Asinof, 1971; Barbara Grizzuti Harrison, 1973) and finally the “screwing for virginity” form, quoted by a corporal in the Windsor Star in 1978 (Popik ↗).

After 2008 — George Carlin died on 22 June 2008, and georgecarlin.net ↗ observes that, as with other bogus Carlin quotes, people appear not to have started crediting him with this one until after his death.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest appearance of the exact “screwing for virginity” wording in Barry Popik’s chronology. Earlier citations, from 1968 onward, carry the same joke with different verbs — raping, making out, fucking, fornicating, balling — which is itself evidence that the line grew out of protest culture rather than a scripted routine.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted. The wording has no identified author and no identified first publication of its own — it circulated as an anonymous protest slogan and was recorded, in varying forms, by newspapers and books that each carry their own separate copyrights. Quoting the sentence itself is a short quotation of an ownerless saying; the surrounding passages transcribed above belong to their publishers.

author.name: George Carlin
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned to
author.heading: Not the author: George Carlin
author.metaLine: 1937–2008 · American comedian, satirist and social critic
author.bio: George Carlin (May 12, 1937 – June 22, 2008) was an American comedian, satirist, social critic, actor and author who recorded fourteen stand-up specials for HBO. He is also one of the internet’s most heavily forged bylines — Wikipedia’s article ↗ notes that many joke lists and rants have been falsely attributed to him, often contradicting what he actually thought. In 2001 Carlin posted an essay on his own site asking people to stop, and gave a rule of thumb: treat nothing online as his unless it came from one of his albums, books, HBO specials, or his website. By that test, this saying is not his.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why none of it holds
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook magnet quote: an ownerless slogan that keeps getting handed to whichever famous rude truth-teller is nearest.

items.why: Barry Popik states there is no evidence the saying originated in any Carlin routine, and georgecarlin.net ↗ lists it among bogus Carlin quotations, noting it turns up on none of his albums, HBO specials or books and that people appear not to have started crediting him until after he died. Aggregators still run it under his name — Goodreads ↗ among them.
Popik notes the saying is sometimes given to Bruce (1925–1966) as well, but that he died before the saying was first recorded ↗.
georgecarlin.net ↗ mentions research going back to 2002 crediting the line to Emma S. Riches, but calls the attribution “a little iffy.” The documented print record starts in 1968.

misattribution.truthLine: No one owns it. It is an anonymous Vietnam-era protest saying, in print since 19 May 1968 and shape-shifting through half a dozen verbs before settling on this one — see Barry Popik’s chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why a slogan with no author travelled so far
lead: Before it was anyone’s punchline it was public property. Barry Popik’s chronology tracks the saying across picket signs, campus graffiti, a latrine wall at Chu Lai, letters to the editor and mimeographed underground papers — and across at least six different verbs. In 1969 the magazine Liberation could credit it only to “an underground pundit.”

That shapelessness is the tell. A line with a real author arrives fixed; this one arrived in whatever form the sign-painter needed, hardening into the “screwing for virginity” version only later. Folk sayings drift, and drifting sayings eventually land on the most famous plausible name in the room. For a blunt, obscene, antiwar one-liner in the English-speaking internet, that name was always going to be George Carlin.
context.detailsSummary: The variants Popik documents, in order
detailsBody: 1968 — “raping for love” (student picket sign, Omaha Sunday World-Herald). 1969 — “making out for chastity” (campus graffito, Salina Journal) and “fucking for chastity” (Liberation, vol. 14). 1970 — “raping for chastity” (a Chu Lai latrine, The Enterprise) and “fornicating for chastity” (Fond du Lac Commonwealth Reporter).

1971 — “balling for virginity” (Eliot Asinof, Craig and Joan: Two Lives for Peace, p. 223). 1973 — “fucking for virginity” on a children’s hand-lettered poster (Barbara Grizzuti Harrison, Unlearning the Lie: Sexism in School, p. 19). 1978 — “screwing for virginity,” quoted by a corporal in the Windsor Star. All per Popik’s chronology ↗.
context.pull: Six different verbs, one joke, no author. That is what a real folk saying looks like.
